name: Neck fillers / skin boosters

lead: Neck fillers and skin boosters are injectable treatments, usually hyaluronic acid, used to soften horizontal neck lines (sometimes called necklace lines) and improve the quality of neck skin. The smoothing is visible after treatment.

A clinician injects the gel into or beneath the skin to add volume or hydration to creased areas. The sources reviewed are clinical-trial registrations, including a 26-person study of Restylane Refyne for horizontal neck lines and a 146-person study of a hyaluronic acid filler for anti-aging performance and tolerance, without published results.

paras: Treatment is done in a clinic by a trained injector, and the filler is placed in the neck lines or distributed across the skin as a booster. It is discussed in aesthetic-medicine and looksmaxxing circles as a non-surgical option for a younger-looking neck.
Risks were not described in the sources reviewed. Fillers are administered by clinicians, and product regulation varies by country.

angle.text: Hyaluronic acid fillers and skin boosters are injected to hydrate and plump neck skin and soften horizontal necklace lines, with smoothing visible after treatment. Registered trials include a 26-person study of Restylane Refyne for neck lines.

lead: Neck fillers and skin boosters are clinician-administered injectables, most often hyaluronic acid (HA) gels, used to soften horizontal neck lines (sometimes called necklace lines) and improve the texture, hydration and firmness of neck skin. People use them to make the neck look smoother and more youthful so it matches the face, a common concern as the neck is often one of the first places age shows.

Two approaches are grouped under the name. Cross-linked HA fillers add structure and soften creases, while skin boosters are lighter HA or related products placed in the dermis to improve hydration, elasticity and overall skin quality rather than to add visible volume.[1] An expert consensus on non-animal stabilised HA skin boosters describes a typical plan of up to three initial sessions followed by a maintenance schedule at 4 to 6 month intervals, with skin texture continuing to improve for up to 12 months after repeat treatment.[2]

Published neck-specific research found is mainly in the form of registered trials, including a 26-participant Restylane Refyne study of horizontal neck rhytides, alongside broader reviews of skin boosters and filler procedures.[3][4][5]

The US FDA's dermal filler guidance lists the neck among areas where it recommends against injecting fillers, and its approved uses cover the face and back of the hands; practitioners and registered trials nonetheless study neck treatment.[6][3]
infobox: Cross-linked HA fillers; HA skin boosters; biostimulators such as poly-L-lactic acid
Up to 3 initial sessions, then maintenance every 4-6 months (expert panel)[2]
Fillers are medical devices (US FDA, UK/EU CE mark)[7]

paras: Dermal fillers are injectable substances placed into the skin and underlying tissue, mostly to smooth wrinkles, restore volume and shape features; HA is among the most common because it occurs naturally in the body, is biodegradable, and most products are cross-linked to last longer.[7] The effect of fillers is temporary and is usually described as lasting around six months, depending on the product, the individual's skin and the injector.[7]

Skin boosters are a newer use of HA and related materials. A 2024 overview describes them as injectables for dull, dehydrated, less elastic ageing skin, made from materials that include collagen, hyaluronic acid, amino acids, polycaprolactone, polydeoxyribonucleotide, poly-L-lactic acid and botulinum neurotoxin, with needle-free jet injection also discussed.[1] Reviews list other injectable materials used as boosters, including polynucleotides, PDLLA and exosome-based products.[8]

A 2024 review in Skin Research and Technology describes the skin-booster concept as a shift from using HA fillers mainly to add volume towards delivering HA directly to the dermis to treat skin condition, with reported benefits including hydration, elasticity and wrinkle reduction.[9]

The neck's horizontal lines, sometimes called necklace lines, together with crepey texture and reduced firmness, are among the signs of ageing people seek to treat so the neck matches the face. A 2025 comprehensive review of surgical and non-surgical rejuvenation techniques covers the range from injectables to surgery.[10]

Wrinkle treatment with HA depends on the filler's firmness and depth of placement. Wikipedia says superficial and mid-dermal placement is used for fine lines, while firmer fillers go deeper for severe wrinkles, and that exercise can shorten how long fillers last.[7]

Surgical neck lifts address the same concern from another direction. Wikipedia describes platysmaplasty, which tightens or repositions the platysma muscle, as a common part of neck lift surgery, and notes that skin loses elasticity as collagen and elastin decline and that the platysma can separate and form vertical bands with a less defined jawline.[11] Injectables, in contrast, target skin lines and skin quality rather than muscle position.

Neck treatment targets horizontal rhytides, the creases that run across the neck, and general crepiness or dullness of neck skin. A registered trial evaluated Restylane Refyne for correction of horizontal neck rhytides in 26 participants.[3] Another registered study tested a HA-based filler containing a vitamin, mineral and amino-acid complex, NCTF135HA, for anti-ageing performance and tolerance in 146 participants.[4]

Injections are given by clinicians, and an expert panel describing skin-booster practice notes that products placed in the dermis are intended to restore hydration and stimulate collagen, which in turn supports skin density.[2] Some practitioners combine injectables with energy devices; a registered trial examined Ultherapy after Sculptra treatment for skin laxity.[5]

Practitioners discuss neck rejuvenation as layered. A 2025 case-report article on multilayer rejuvenation notes that clinicians divide facial ageing into upper face, midface, lower face and neck regions and combine surgical options and energy-based devices with injectables.[12] Registered work reflects this, including a study of Ultherapy after Sculptra for skin laxity.[5] Fillers are described as distinct from neurotoxins such as Botox.[7]

Common reactions to fillers include bruising, redness, pain and itching; less often infection or allergic reaction occurs, and rare serious complications include vascular occlusion with tissue necrosis or, in the face, vision loss.[7] Regulators treat fillers as medical devices; in the US injection is by or under a licensed provider and in the UK and EU a larger number of products are marketed under CE marking.[7]

A 2025 narrative review of anti-ageing procedures discusses effectiveness and potential side effects across surgical and non-surgical options.[10] Individual pain and technique questions, such as intradermal versus subdermal placement of PDLLA boosters, have been examined in randomised split-injection research on the face.[13]

The FDA's dermal filler page lists unintended injection into a blood vessel as the most serious risk, which can cause tissue death, vision problems including blindness and stroke, and notes that complications may be permanent. It reports bruising, redness, swelling, pain and itching as common, nodules, infection and allergic reaction as less common, and rare anaphylaxis, migration and death. The page states approved uses are face and back of the hand, and that the agency recommends against injecting fillers in the glabella, nose, periorbital area, forehead and neck. It advises seeing a licensed provider experienced in dermatology or plastic surgery, says no fillers are approved for over-the-counter use, and warns about counterfeit products sold online.[6]

Wikipedia reports that fillers are regulated differently across regions: in the EEA and UK they are non-prescription medical devices requiring a CE mark, which does not require a demonstration of medical efficacy, and it states there are over 140 injectable fillers in the UK and European market against six approved in the US.[7] The FDA page says approved uses in the US cover adults 22 and older for facial wrinkles and folds, lip, cheek, chin and back-of-hand augmentation, and that no fillers are approved for over-the-counter use.[6]

A completed registered trial (NCT04162496) evaluated Restylane Refyne for horizontal neck rhytides in 26 participants.[3] A completed registered study (NCT05609617) assessed NCTF135HA in 146 participants, and another (NCT01422538) studied Ultherapy after Sculptra for skin laxity in 30 participants.[4][5] The registry entries do not report results, so effect sizes are not given here.

Beyond the neck, an expert panel consensus on non-animal stabilised HA skin boosters recommends an initial series followed by maintenance and reports progressive skin-texture improvement for up to 12 months after repeat treatment at 4 to 6 month intervals.[2] A 2024 overview of injectable skin boosters reviews their types, mechanisms and clinical uses.[1]

Controlled facial studies of boosters give a sense of the outcomes measured in this field. A 2026 randomised, split-face, double-blinded trial in 20 adults with cheek roughness compared an injectable acellular dermal matrix with HA on the opposite side over 20 weeks, assessing density, elasticity, wrinkle depth and hydration; the authors report greater improvement on the matrix side.[14] A 2026 split-injection trial in 21 participants found intradermal PDLLA injections were rated more painful than subdermal ones (mean visual analogue scores 6.18 versus 3.85).[13] These trials treated the face rather than the neck.

Other injectables placed for skin quality include poly-L-lactic acid and poly-D,L-lactic acid, which stimulate collagen as they degrade rather than adding immediate volume,[7] polynucleotides and exosome-based products.[8] A 2026 randomised split-injection study compared pain with intradermal versus subdermal PDLLA booster injection.[13]

lore.intro: Neck fillers and skin boosters are discussed mainly in clinical and trial literature rather than in looksmaxxing forums, where the neck appears more often in jawline and fat-reduction threads. The claims below are those made by clinicians and product developers.[2][1]

claims.claim: HA skin boosters improve skin hydration, elasticity and texture, including over repeated sessions.
Neck lines can be softened with HA filler.
Boosters differ from fillers by treating skin quality rather than volume.
Filler complications are rare and manageable.

timeline.event: A registered trial begins testing Ultherapy following Sculptra treatment for skin laxity.[5]
An expert panel publishes a consensus on non-animal stabilised HA as a skin quality booster.[2]
A registered study of the NCTF135HA filler for anti-ageing performance and tolerance begins, enrolling 146 participants.[4]
A registered trial of Restylane Refyne for horizontal neck rhytides begins.[3]
Randomised split-face and split-injection booster trials are published, on the face.[14][13]
